knowledgeUnits.heading: DDL changes structure

leadVisual.title: Distinguish a new attribute from a new value

coreExplanation: Data Definition Language defines and modifies database structure. It can create a database, define a table's attributes and constraints, or alter an existing table definition. These operations determine what data the database can store.
Creating a Loan table does not add a particular loan record. Similarly, adding DueDate changes the permitted structure for loan records rather than choosing the date for one member's loan.

knowledgeUnits.heading: DML retrieves and maintains records

leadVisual.title: DML works with records

coreExplanation: Data Manipulation Language works with records in the defined structure. SELECT retrieves specified information. INSERT INTO adds records, UPDATE changes stored field values, and DELETE FROM removes records.

A query can produce a result table without altering the stored rows. Updating one member's phone number changes data while leaving the Member field definitions intact. These are both DML operations in the syllabus classification.

knowledgeUnits.heading: SQL expresses both kinds of operation

leadVisual.title: SQL includes both DDL and DML

coreExplanation: Structured Query Language (SQL) is the industry-standard language used for both DDL and DML. The DBMS interprets SQL statements and carries out their requested changes or queries. DDL and DML describe roles within SQL rather than two alternative database products.

Determine the category from the requested effect, not from the word 'change' alone. A SQL statement that changes a column's definition is structural; one that changes the current value in that column operates on data.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read the supplied statement before explaining it

leadVisual.title: Read what each SQL clause asks for

coreExplanation: A SQL statement must be interpreted from the actual identifiers, conditions and values supplied. In a retrieval statement, SELECT identifies output expressions, FROM identifies the source and WHERE restricts rows. A changed field list can alter the columns without changing which records qualify.

Read a definition statement by identifying the object created or altered, its field types and its constraints. Quoted text literals represent values rather than field names. Explain the effect of the operator or limit given; recognising a keyword alone does not determine the result.

leadVisual.title: Create the database before defining its tables

coreExplanation: CREATE DATABASE creates a named database in a DBMS that supports this SQL operation. The name is an identifier, not a quoted data value. Creating the database does not by itself define its tables or populate records.

After creating SchoolLibrary, the developer selects that database in the chosen DBMS interface and defines its tables. The interface command for selecting a database varies between products; the SQL statement below expresses the required creation operation.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose data types and define fields

leadVisual.title: Choose a type from the meaning of a value

coreExplanation: Choose a field type from the meaning and range of its values. CHARACTER stores fixed-length character data; VARCHAR(n) stores text up to the specified maximum length. INTEGER represents whole numbers, REAL represents values with a fractional part, and BOOLEAN represents true or false.

DATE and TIME represent calendar dates and times of day separately. Field names and types appear inside the CREATE TABLE brackets, separated by commas. A numeric-looking identifier may still need a text type when leading zeroes or non-arithmetic meaning must be preserved.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Alter an existing table definition

leadVisual.title: ALTER TABLE adds a field to the definition

coreExplanation: ALTER TABLE changes the structure of an existing table. To add Email to the Student definition, identify the existing table and supply the new field name and type after ADD. Existing student records remain present.

In this example the added Email field is nullable and has no default, so existing records initially have no supplied email value. Setting an email for one student is a later UPDATE operation. The new attribute and the value in one occurrence are separate changes.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Declare the primary key

leadVisual.title: A primary key identifies each record

coreExplanation: A PRIMARY KEY constraint declares the chosen identifier for a table. The key must distinguish every record and cannot be null. Write the selected field inside PRIMARY KEY brackets in the CREATE TABLE definition.

A composite primary key lists all fields needed for identification, for example PRIMARY KEY (StudentID, ClubID) in Membership. The combination must be unique; either component may recur in other combinations. Choose the key from the stated business rules.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Declare the referenced relationship

leadVisual.title: Declare which field references which key

coreExplanation: FOREIGN KEY names the field or fields in the current table; REFERENCES names the related table and referenced key. In Student, FOREIGN KEY (TutorID) REFERENCES Tutor(TutorID) declares which parent identifier each non-null tutor reference must match.

Create the referenced table and key first when using this teaching sequence. The child field may repeat when many students share a tutor. A foreign-key declaration enforces the link; it does not automatically assign a tutor or create the missing parent record.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose the result columns and source

leadVisual.title: SELECT chooses the output columns

coreExplanation: SELECT lists the fields or expressions required in the result, while FROM names the source table. Returning MemberName alone does not return MemberID or Active. Reading a result leaves the original Member records unchanged.

Use the Member and Loan data in this lesson to trace each request. Each example states any required ordering explicitly; without ORDER BY, a DBMS need not return records in insertion or primary-key order.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Filter rows using a Boolean condition

leadVisual.title: WHERE: both conditions must be true

coreExplanation: WHERE retains only records for which the condition is true. Combine comparisons with AND when all conditions must hold, or OR when an alternative is sufficient. Parentheses make the intended grouping explicit in compound expressions.
The Loan example requires an unreturned loan and a fee of at least 3. Loan 202 has a sufficient fee but is returned; loan 201 is unreturned but its fee is only 2. Neither satisfies both conditions.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Sort the returned records

leadVisual.title: ORDER BY rearranges the result rows

coreExplanation: ORDER BY arranges result rows by the specified field or expression. ASC means increasing order and is the default; DESC means decreasing order. Sorting changes result presentation rather than the stored values.

Multiple sort fields are applied in sequence: sort by the first field, then use the next field for ties. The example sorts fees from largest to smallest and uses LoanID ascending to make any equal-fee ordering predictable.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Form groups before calculating group results

leadVisual.title: GROUP BY forms one group per key value

coreExplanation: GROUP BY places records sharing the grouping values into the same group. An aggregate can then calculate one result for each group. Grouping loans by MemberID lets COUNT(*) report the number of loans for each represented member.

Include non-aggregated selected fields in GROUP BY so each returned value has a defined meaning for the group. ORDER BY can subsequently arrange the grouped results; it does not create the groups. A member with no Loan row does not appear in a grouping of Loan alone.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Match records from two tables with INNER JOIN

leadVisual.title: INNER JOIN returns matching row pairs

coreExplanation: An INNER JOIN combines row pairs satisfying its ON condition. Here Member.MemberID = Loan.MemberID connects each loan to its member. Qualify shared field names with the table name to make the intended reference unambiguous.

A member with two loans contributes two joined rows, while a member with no matching loan contributes none. WHERE may further filter the joined rows. These AS SQL tasks use at most two tables; use an explicit INNER JOIN and a separate ON matching condition.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Calculate SUM, COUNT and AVG

leadVisual.title: Aggregates calculate over the selected records

coreExplanation: Expression: SUM(Fee); What it includes: Adds non-null fees.. Expression: COUNT(Fee); What it includes: Counts non-null fees.. Expression: COUNT(*); What it includes: Counts rows, including rows with a null Fee.. Expression: AVG(Fee); What it includes: Mean of included non-null fees..

For fees 2, 4, 6, 0, 3, SUM is 15, COUNT(*) is 5 and AVG is 3. SUM, AVG and COUNT(Fee) ignore null fees. Zero is a known value and stays included. Without GROUP BY, the query gives one overall aggregate result for the selected records.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Insert values into named fields

leadVisual.title: INSERT INTO adds a new record

coreExplanation: INSERT INTO adds a record. Name the target fields and supply the corresponding VALUES in the same order. Text literals use single quotes; numeric and Boolean values are written according to their types.

Check the new primary key and any foreign-key values before insertion. The library example adds MemberID 5 with the name Elena and Active TRUE. It does not alter an existing member's record, and it must fail if that primary key is already present.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Delete only the intended records

leadVisual.title: DELETE FROM removes the selected row

coreExplanation: DELETE FROM removes complete records from the named table. WHERE selects the records to remove. To remove the completed loan with LoanID 204, match that identifier rather than a member identifier shared by several loans.

Without a WHERE condition, deletion targets all rows in the table, subject to constraints. Check the intended rows first with a corresponding SELECT. Removing a referenced parent may be rejected by foreign-key constraints; this example removes the child Loan record.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Change fields while keeping the record

leadVisual.title: UPDATE changes a field in the selected record

coreExplanation: UPDATE names the table, SET supplies the new field values, and WHERE selects the affected records. Updating Returned to TRUE for LoanID 203 leaves that loan's identity, member and fee in place.

A missing or incorrect WHERE condition can affect unintended records. Decide whether the business task requires changing a value or removing a record, then verify both the affected rows and the values that should remain unchanged.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose detail according to the purpose

leadVisual.title: Two purposes, different relevant facts

coreExplanation: Abstraction removes unnecessary detail while retaining the essential features of a problem or system. What counts as essential depends on the purpose: a journey planner needs connections and travel times, whereas a vehicle-painting system may need colours.

A simpler representation reduces the information a designer must consider and makes the important relationships easier to understand. It can also reduce the data and processing needed by the solution. Omitting a detail that changes the required result makes the model unsuitable, even if the model becomes smaller.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Produce and check an abstract model

knowledgeUnits.heading: Execute dependent operations in order

leadVisual.title: A sequence with a dependency

coreExplanation: Sequence executes instructions in their written order. A later calculation may depend on an earlier input or assignment, so moving operations can change the result or read an unassigned variable. Follow dependencies when placing statements.

For a price calculation, input the quantity before multiplying it by the unit price, then add any fixed charge before outputting the final amount. Declarations can appear first to document types, but they do not perform those calculations.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose the correct branch

leadVisual.title: A mark selects one of two outcomes

coreExplanation: Selection chooses operations according to a Boolean condition. In IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF, a true condition selects the THEN block and a false condition selects the ELSE block. Execution continues after ENDIF once the selected block finishes.

Write a condition that matches the exact boundary in the requirement. A pass mark of at least 50 uses Mark >= 50. Mark = 50 would accept only the boundary value and reject higher marks; Mark > 50 would incorrectly reject 50 itself.

workedExample.title: Select a result at an inclusive boundary

knowledgeUnits.heading: Repeat with a defined stopping rule

leadVisual.title: Choose a loop from the requirement

coreExplanation: Iteration repeats a block of operations. A FOR loop is suitable when the number of repetitions is known. A WHILE loop tests a condition before the body, so it may execute zero times. A REPEAT ... UNTIL loop tests after the body and therefore executes at least once.

Initialise totals or counts before the loop, update them inside the loop, and put a final aggregate output after the loop. A condition-controlled loop must make progress towards stopping. In a countdown, decreasing Count eventually makes Count > 0 false.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Place a decision inside a repeated task

leadVisual.title: Count passes from ten marks

coreExplanation: The three constructs cooperate in a complete solution. Counting passes begins with an initialisation, repeats input and a decision for each mark, and finishes with one output. Indentation shows that the decision is inside the loop while the final output is outside it.

Read each new mark during its iteration. Increase the count only on the qualifying branch and leave it unchanged otherwise. This arrangement counts qualifying inputs rather than counting all iterations or checking one old input repeatedly.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Document a solution in structured English

leadVisual.title: Age classification in structured English

coreExplanation: Structured English expresses an algorithm using controlled natural-language steps and clear grouping. State the operations in order, identify both outcomes of a decision and make the scope of any repetition explicit. It should leave the same computational choices determined as pseudocode does.

A flowchart shows that control structure with symbols and directed lines, while pseudocode uses statements and indentation. Changing notation should not change the accepted inputs or results. Trace a value on each side of a boundary when comparing two representations.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use symbols and arrows consistently

leadVisual.title: Standard flowchart symbols

coreExplanation: Use terminators for start and end, parallelograms for input and output, rectangles for processing, and diamonds for decisions. Arrowheads indicate the next operation. Label the outgoing decision paths consistently, for example Yes and No, so the truth value selects an unambiguous route.

A loop needs a return path to its condition or repeated body, according to when it tests. Paths that rejoin must not imply that both selection branches execute. Inspect the arrow direction at the final output as well as at the decision; an output cannot follow an end terminator.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Write pseudocode from a flowchart

leadVisual.title: A loop returns to its condition

coreExplanation: Begin at the start symbol and follow the arrows. Translate each input, process and output into its corresponding statement. At a decision, retain the full expression and place each path's operations in the appropriate block. Declare suitable types for the data used by the resulting program.

In the displayed countdown, a false condition goes directly to the final message. A true condition outputs the current value, decreases it and returns to the same test. That control flow corresponds to WHILE, with the message placed after ENDWHILE.

leadVisual.title: Before combining the conditions

coreExplanation: Efficient pseudocode avoids unnecessary operations while remaining correct and understandable. Look for repeated calculations, repeated tests with unchanged operands and avoidable traversals. Meaningful identifiers and indentation support review, but a shorter line count alone does not establish fewer operations.

In the example, Mark is read once and is not changed between two identical Mark >= 50 tests. The first test increments Count and the second displays Pass. Both operations can share one true branch. This reduces two comparisons to one for every run while retaining the action order and final count.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Refactor and check behavioural equivalence

leadVisual.title: After combining the conditions

coreExplanation: Move both pass-only actions inside one IF Mark >= 50 block, keeping Count's initialisation before the decision and OUTPUT Count afterwards. A failed mark then skips both actions, just as in the original. A passing mark increments before displaying Pass, preserving the observable sequence.

Compare original and revised versions for below-boundary, boundary and above-boundary inputs. Check outputs and updated values, not merely whether execution finishes. Reusable functions can also centralise a rule such as ValidMark, but a function call is not automatically a speed improvement; measure the operation or duplication that the change actually removes.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Purpose and stages of a development life cycle

leadVisual.title: Connect each development activity with the evidence it produces

coreExplanation: A development life cycle coordinates the route from the problem to a tested, maintained solution. Records connect requirements, design decisions and results; following stages alone does not guarantee a suitable product.

Analysis: The problem, user requirements and constraints. Design: Data, algorithms, module interfaces and tests. Coding: An implementation of the design. Testing: Actual behaviour compared with expected results, exposing defects. Maintenance: Changes after delivery as faults, environments and user needs change.
Feedback can reveal a need to revisit earlier work. The chosen development model determines how the team organises these activities.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Waterfall: planned sequential stages

leadVisual.title: A stable payroll rule

coreExplanation: Waterfall completes planned stages largely in sequence. The output of one stage is reviewed before the next proceeds, so requirements and designs provide a documented basis for implementation and testing. It is useful where requirements are well understood and stable and formal approval records are valuable.

The staged structure makes milestones and responsibilities clear. However, users may see working software late, and a requirement change discovered after design or coding can force substantial rework. Returning to earlier work is possible; it undermines the assumption that the earlier stage was settled.

knowledgeUnits.heading: RAD and choosing a suitable model

leadVisual.title: Select using the project constraints

coreExplanation: Rapid application development (RAD) emphasises rapid prototyping, time-boxed development and frequent user involvement. Users inspect early working prototypes and give prompt feedback that changes the next version. Short agreed development periods concentrate effort on a usable result rather than waiting for every feature.

RAD can suit an interactive booking interface when users are available and components can be prototyped quickly. Limited user availability or tightly dependent components can make this approach difficult. A project needing exhaustive assurance and stable approved documentation may find rapid changes harder to control. Choose a model by relating these features to requirement stability, delivery time, user access and assurance needs.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Decompose a problem into a structure chart

leadVisual.title: ProcessOrder: calls and data

coreExplanation: A structure chart records the decomposition of a problem into modules. A rectangle names a module, and a connecting hierarchy line shows a calling relationship. Place the controlling module above the modules it calls, then refine a large subtask into another level when needed. The chart documents the overall design rather than every statement executed inside a module.

For one order, ProcessOrder obtains a positive integer Quantity and a non-negative real UnitPrice, calculates their product and displays the cost. The three child modules have distinct responsibilities. ReadOrder obtains the inputs, CalculateCost returns their product, and DisplayCost presents the supplied amount. For this example the parent calls them in that left-to-right sequence.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Document persistent states and transitions

leadVisual.title: A turnstile has two persistent states

coreExplanation: A state-transition diagram documents the possible conditions of a system and the events that move it between those conditions. It helps a designer communicate behaviour that depends on the current state. An initial-state indicator tells the reader where an event sequence starts.

In the turnstile model, a coin unlocks a locked barrier and passing locks it again. A push while locked leaves it locked. A second coin while already unlocked leaves it unlocked. Each arrow is directed and labelled with an event; a self-loop represents an event that leaves the current state unchanged. More detailed diagrams may add conditions to an event label.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace behaviour and distinguish design documents

leadVisual.title: Follow the turnstile

coreExplanation: Read one event at a time, starting at the initial state. Follow an outgoing arrow whose label matches that event and any stated condition, then use the new state for the next event. An arrow from another state cannot be used merely because its label matches.

A structure chart answers which modules call other modules; a state-transition diagram answers which state changes are possible. A flowchart records processing steps and control flow. These documents can describe different aspects of one system, but none should be read as a substitute for the others. If a required event has no transition from the current state, the diagram needs clarification rather than an invented transition.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Distinguish errors and reduce their likelihood

leadVisual.title: Choose evidence for the fault

coreExplanation: A syntax error breaks the grammar of the language, such as an IF statement without its required ENDIF. A translator or syntax checker can report it. A logic error uses accepted syntax but implements the wrong requirement; execution may finish with an incorrect result. A run-time error occurs during execution, for example an attempted division by zero or opening a file that is not available.

Clear requirements, modular design, meaningful identifiers, consistent indentation and review help avoid faults. Validate input where required, check preconditions before risky operations and use complete constructs. These practices reduce risk but do not prove a program fault-free. Tests, traces and diagnostics provide evidence about particular behaviours.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Expose a failure and locate its cause

leadVisual.title: Trace the faulty pass decision

coreExplanation: Begin with a specific input, an expected result derived from the requirement and the actual result. Reproduce the mismatch, then narrow the search using translator messages, a manual trace or debugger evidence. A diagnostic line may be where the failure becomes visible rather than where the incorrect value originated.

For a pass rule of at least 50, trace the complete selection with Mark equal to 50. In the supplied faulty program, Mark > 50 evaluates to FALSE and the ELSE branch assigns Fail. This identifies the comparison as the cause. A condition Mark < 50 is not inherently faulty: it would be correct for a Fail branch with a Pass alternative.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Dry runs and walkthroughs

leadVisual.title: Dry run with inputs 4, -2, 3

coreExplanation: A dry run manually follows an algorithm with selected input data. Record changing variables, decisions and output in a trace table; use the actual statements, including initialisation and loop limits. This can expose logic faults without running the program on a computer.

A walkthrough is a structured review in which the author explains the design or code to others. Participants follow representative cases, question assumptions and record faults or omissions. A walkthrough can include a manual trace, but the collaborative discussion is distinct from a person carrying out a dry run alone.

knowledgeUnits.heading: White-box and black-box test design

leadVisual.title: Two reasons to choose a case

coreExplanation: White-box testing uses knowledge of the internal code structure to choose test cases, for example inputs that make a decision true and false. Coverage evidence records which branches or paths have executed. Exercising every branch is useful but does not prove that every requirement was implemented.

Black-box testing derives inputs and expected outputs from the specification without relying on the internal algorithm. For a 10% member discount, tests should distinguish a member from a non-member and compare the amount due with the specified calculation. Both approaches can use the same input values; what differs is the reason for selecting them.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Alpha, beta and acceptance testing

leadVisual.title: Choose the method for the purpose

coreExplanation: Alpha testing takes place under developer control before wider release, using internal testers and sometimes user representatives to expose faults in a controlled setting. Beta testing gives a near-complete version to selected external users in their own realistic environments, where different devices and usage patterns can reveal additional problems.

Acceptance testing checks the delivered system against agreed user requirements so the customer can decide whether to accept it. Select cases that demonstrate those requirements, rather than treating all user feedback as acceptance evidence. Beta feedback can be broad and uneven, while acceptance checks need explicit pass conditions linked to the agreed system.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Plan the overall testing approach

leadVisual.title: An outline strategy for room bookings

coreExplanation: A test strategy sets the overall approach: what will be tested, which levels and methods will be used, the sequence of work, responsibilities, resources and conditions for starting or finishing a phase. It helps a team coordinate testing and decide how the evidence will address project risks and requirements.

For a room-booking program, individual module checks can precede integration tests of the availability and booking modules. Customer acceptance can then use agreed booking rules. Naming a method alone is insufficient planning: identify who performs it, what environment or data it needs, and what results allow work to proceed.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Why maintenance continues after delivery

leadVisual.title: Control a post-release change

coreExplanation: Maintenance keeps a delivered system useful as its circumstances change. Real use can expose faults missed by pre-release tests. New operating systems, equipment, regulations or external interfaces may require adaptation. Users may also need additional features or better performance after the original requirements have been met.

A requested change should be understood before editing. Identify affected modules, data and interfaces, then check the revised behaviour and relevant existing functions. Keep the request, change and test evidence connected so later maintainers can understand why the system behaves as it does.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 9: Algorithm design and problem-solving

leadVisual.title: S9 review route

coreExplanation: Begin with the required result and retain the facts that determine it. Decompose the task into cooperating responsibilities, choose meaningful identifiers and refine the processing until the rules and execution order are explicit. The resulting IPO, pseudocode and flowchart should describe the same solution.

Challenge a completed algorithm at decision boundaries and loop limits. Follow each path using actual values, checking initialisation, new inputs, updates and the final output. A convincing design combines correct logic with a representation that another programmer can implement without guessing.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 10: Data types and structures

leadVisual.title: S10 review route

coreExplanation: Choose each value's type before grouping values: record fields may have different types, whereas an array has a declared element type and explicit bounds. One index selects a 1D element; two select a 2D element. Write complete declarations, field access and bounded iteration before tracing the resulting values.

For array processing, linear search checks consecutive elements and reports a matching position or absence; bubble sort uses complete adjacent swaps. Files retain results between runs through the appropriate read, write or append mode. ADTs specify data and operations: use LIFO for a stack, FIFO for a queue and links for a linked list, and keep the array implementation's active state consistent after each operation.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 11: Programming

leadVisual.title: Programming review checks

coreExplanation: Translate the stated rules into declarations, expressions and correctly placed control structures. Read supplied routine interfaces before calling them. A complete solution defines values before use, respects condition boundaries and makes progress toward the stopping condition.

Connect subprograms through arguments, returned values and intentional reference updates. In this review, a parking session costs 3 per whole hour; positive integer hours are entered until sentinel zero. A charge function returns each fee and an accumulation procedure updates the running total. The first input may already be zero.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 12: Software development

leadVisual.title: S12 review route

coreExplanation: Connect each development decision to observable evidence: requirements and project constraints guide the life cycle; a hierarchy and labelled interfaces guide implementation; states and transitions document event-dependent behaviour. Use a trace to check that the resulting algorithm implements the intended rules.

Choose tests for the risks being examined and record their expected results before running them. After delivery, identify why a change is needed, analyse its impact, make the requested amendment and check both changed and preserved behaviour. A category name alone cannot demonstrate any of these practical skills.
